text:
Condition: Acne and Rosacea

General guidance:
- Avoid harsh scrubbing, strong exfoliants, or alcohol-based products, as these can worsen irritation.
- Use a gentle, fragrance-free cleanser and non-comedogenic moisturizer.
- Avoid touching or picking at the affected area, as this can increase irritation and scarring risk.
- For rosacea-prone skin, triggers like spicy food, alcohol, extreme temperatures, and sun exposure may worsen redness — sunscreen is generally recommended.
- A dermatologist can help identify the right long-term routine and whether further evaluation is needed.

Condition: Atopic Dermatitis

General guidance:
- Keep skin well moisturized with a fragrance-free moisturizer, especially after bathing.
- Avoid long, hot showers and harsh soaps, which can dry out and irritate the skin further.
- Identify and avoid personal triggers such as certain fabrics, stress, or environmental allergens where possible.
- Keep fingernails short to reduce skin damage from scratching.
- A dermatologist can help build a long-term skincare routine suited to sensitive, atopic-prone skin.

Condition: Cellulitis, Impetigo and other Bacterial Infections

General guidance:
- Keep the affected area clean and covered with a clean, breathable bandage if possible.
- Avoid touching, scratching, or draining the area yourself.
- Wash hands frequently to avoid spreading the infection to other areas or people.
- Watch for spreading redness, warmth, swelling, or fever, as these can indicate the infection is worsening.
- Bacterial skin infections, especially cellulitis, should be evaluated by a doctor promptly, as they can spread quickly.

Condition: Seborrheic Keratoses and other Benign Tumors

General guidance:
- These growths are often harmless, but any new or changing growth is still worth having checked.
- Avoid picking, scratching, or attempting to remove the growth at home.
- Track any changes in size, color, or texture over time.
- Protect the area from unnecessary friction (e.g., from clothing or jewelry).
- A dermatologist can confirm whether the growth is benign and whether monitoring or removal is appropriate.

Condition: Bullous Disease

General guidance:
- Avoid friction, tight clothing, or activities that could rupture blisters, as this increases risk of infection.
- Keep the area clean and avoid popping blisters yourself.
- Loose, soft clothing can help reduce irritation on affected skin.
- Track how quickly new blisters appear and where, as this pattern is useful for a specialist.
- Bullous conditions often need prompt dermatologist evaluation, especially if blisters are spreading or the area is large.

Condition: Contact Dermatitis (including Poison Ivy)

General guidance:
- Try to identify and avoid the substance that triggered the reaction (plants, soaps, metals, fragrances, etc.).
- Gently rinse the affected area with cool water and avoid scrubbing.
- Avoid tight clothing or fabrics that may rub against the irritated skin.
- Keep the area clean and avoid scratching, as this can lead to further irritation or infection.
- If the reaction is spreading, swelling significantly, or affecting the face/eyes, seek medical attention promptly.

Condition: Eczema

General guidance:
- Moisturize frequently, especially after bathing, to help maintain the skin barrier.
- Avoid harsh soaps, fragranced products, and very hot water, which can worsen dryness and irritation.
- Identify and avoid personal triggers such as certain fabrics, allergens, or stress where possible.
- Keep nails trimmed to minimize skin damage from scratching.
- A dermatologist can help build a long-term routine and identify triggers specific to your skin.

Condition: Exanthems and Drug Eruptions

General guidance:
- If a new rash appeared after starting a new medication, note the timing and mention it to a doctor as soon as possible.
- Avoid further exposure to any suspected trigger substance until evaluated.
- Keep the area clean and avoid scratching to reduce irritation.
- Track whether the rash is spreading, and note any fever or feeling unwell alongside it.
- Widespread rashes, especially with fever or blistering, should be evaluated by a doctor promptly.

Condition: Fungal Infections (Tinea, Ringworm, Candidiasis)

General guidance:
- Keep the affected area clean and dry, since fungal infections thrive in warm, moist environments.
- Avoid sharing towels, clothing, or personal items to reduce spread to others.
- Wear breathable fabrics and change out of sweaty clothing promptly.
- Avoid scratching the area, as this can spread the infection to other parts of the body.
- A dermatologist can confirm the type of fungal infection and the right treatment approach.

Condition: Hair Loss / Alopecia

General guidance:
- Avoid tight hairstyles, excessive heat styling, or harsh chemical treatments, which can add stress to hair and scalp.
- Gentle handling of hair when washing or brushing can help reduce further loss.
- Track the pattern of hair loss (patches vs. overall thinning) and how long it has been happening.
- Stress, diet, and overall health can all play a role, so general wellbeing is worth paying attention to.
- A dermatologist can help identify the type of hair loss and appropriate next steps.

Condition: Urticaria (Hives)

General guidance:
- Try to identify possible triggers such as certain foods, heat, stress, or new products, and avoid them where possible.
- Loose, breathable clothing can help reduce irritation on affected skin.
- Avoid hot showers or scratching, as both can worsen itching and swelling.
- Cool compresses may help ease discomfort in the affected area.
- If hives are associated with difficulty breathing, swelling of the face/lips, or spread rapidly, seek emergency medical care immediately — this can be a sign of a serious allergic reaction.

Condition: Scabies, Lyme Disease and other Infestations/Bites

General guidance:
- Avoid close skin contact and sharing clothing or bedding with others until evaluated, as some infestations are contagious.
- Wash clothing and bedding in hot water if scabies or similar infestation is suspected.
- For tick bites or suspected Lyme disease, note the date of the bite and watch for a spreading rash, fever, or fatigue.
- Avoid scratching, as this can lead to secondary skin infection.
- Prompt medical evaluation is recommended, especially for tick-related exposure or spreading rashes.

Condition: Lupus and other Connective Tissue Diseases

General guidance:
- These conditions can involve more than the skin, so ongoing changes in energy, joints, or overall health should also be mentioned to a doctor.
- Sun exposure can trigger flare-ups for some connective tissue conditions, so sun protection (sunscreen, hats, shade) is generally advisable.
- Avoid harsh or irritating skincare products on affected areas.
- Keep a simple log of when symptoms appear or worsen, as this is useful information for a specialist.
- A dermatologist or rheumatologist should evaluate these conditions, as they often require coordinated care.

Condition: Actinic Keratosis, Basal Cell Carcinoma and other Malignant Lesions (High Risk)

General guidance:
- Avoid direct sun exposure and use broad-spectrum sunscreen and protective clothing consistently going forward.
- Do not attempt to treat, pick at, or remove the area yourself.
- Track any changes in size, shape, color, or whether the area bleeds or doesn't heal.
- Avoid tanning beds and prolonged unprotected sun exposure.
- This finding is flagged as higher risk — please prioritize seeing a dermatologist as soon as possible for a full evaluation.

Condition: Melanoma, Skin Cancer, Nevi and Moles (High Risk)

General guidance:
- Avoid direct sun exposure, especially during peak hours, and use broad-spectrum sunscreen and protective clothing.
- Do not attempt to treat, remove, or alter the area yourself.
- Track the ABCDE signs — Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter change, and Evolving appearance — and note any changes.
- Avoid tanning beds and prolonged unprotected sun exposure going forward.
- This finding is flagged as higher risk — please prioritize seeing a dermatologist as soon as possible for a full evaluation.

Condition: Nail Fungus and other Nail Disease

General guidance:
- Keep nails clean, dry, and trimmed, as moisture can worsen fungal nail conditions.
- Avoid sharing nail clippers, files, or footwear to reduce spread.
- Wear breathable footwear and moisture-wicking socks if the feet are affected.
- Avoid picking at or cutting into the affected nail, as this can worsen the condition or cause infection.
- A dermatologist can confirm the cause and appropriate care for persistent nail changes.

Condition: Light Diseases and Disorders of Pigmentation

General guidance:
- Protect the affected area from direct sun exposure using broad-spectrum sunscreen and covering clothing, since pigmentation changes can be more sensitive to UV light.
- Avoid harsh scrubbing, bleaching creams, or unregulated skin-lightening products, as these can irritate the skin further.
- Keep a simple, gentle skincare routine and avoid frequent changes of products.
- Track any changes in size, shape, or color of the affected area and note when it started.
- A dermatologist can properly evaluate the type of pigmentation change and the right next steps.

Condition: Psoriasis, Lichen Planus, and related conditions

General guidance:
- Moisturize regularly to help reduce dryness and scaling associated with these conditions.
- Avoid known personal triggers such as stress, certain medications, or skin injury, which can worsen flare-ups for some people.
- Gentle sun exposure may help some skin conditions, but always use sun protection and avoid burning.
- Avoid picking or scratching plaques, as this can worsen the area (Koebner phenomenon).
- A dermatologist can help create a long-term management plan tailored to the specific condition.

Condition: Herpes, HPV and other Sexually Transmitted Skin Conditions

General guidance:
- Avoid skin-to-skin or sexual contact with the affected area until it has been evaluated, to reduce risk of transmission.
- Keep the area clean and avoid touching or picking at it.
- These conditions are common and manageable — a healthcare provider can offer confidential, judgment-free evaluation and guidance.
- Partner communication and testing may be recommended once you've spoken with a healthcare provider.
- A doctor or sexual health clinic can provide proper evaluation and next steps.

Condition: Systemic Disease (skin signs of a broader internal condition)

General guidance:
- Skin changes linked to systemic disease are often a sign that the whole body should be evaluated, not just the skin.
- Keep track of any other symptoms (fatigue, fever, joint pain, weight changes) and mention them to a doctor.
- Avoid self-treating the skin symptom in isolation, since the underlying cause may need broader medical attention.
- Maintain a gentle skincare routine and avoid irritating the affected area further.
- A general physician or dermatologist should be consulted for a full evaluation.

Condition: Vascular Tumors

General guidance:
- Avoid trauma or friction to the area, as vascular growths can sometimes bleed if irritated.
- Track any changes in size, color, or texture over time and note when the growth first appeared.
- Avoid picking at or attempting to treat the area with home remedies.
- Protect the area from sun exposure if it is in a commonly exposed location.
- A dermatologist should evaluate vascular growths to determine their nature and whether monitoring or further care is needed.

Condition: Vasculitis

General guidance:
- Vasculitis can be linked to broader health conditions, so any accompanying symptoms (fever, joint pain, fatigue) should also be mentioned to a doctor.
- Avoid activities that put extra pressure or friction on affected areas.
- Keep track of when new spots or patches appear and how they change over time.
- Avoid self-treating the skin in isolation, since evaluation of overall health may be needed.
- A doctor should evaluate vasculitis promptly, as it can sometimes indicate an underlying condition needing attention.

Condition: Warts, Molluscum and other Viral Skin Infections

General guidance:
- Avoid picking, scratching, or shaving over the affected area, as this can spread the infection to other areas.
- Avoid sharing towels, razors, or personal items to reduce spread to others.
- Keep the area clean and avoid unnecessary touching.
- These infections are common and often resolve over time, but persistent or spreading lesions should be evaluated.
- A dermatologist can advise on appropriate care and whether removal is recommended.
